title: Dynamical Classification System for Recursive Collapse in Autoregressive Language Models
abstract: Abstract We introduce MASSIF (Multiscale Attractor Stability & Stress Inference Framework), a latent telemetry system for measuring hidden-state dynamics in autoregressive language models. Across 12 architectures - GPT-2 family (Small, Medium, Large, XL), Bloom-560M, TinyLlama-1.1B, DeepSeek-1.3B, Gemma-2-2B, Qwen2-0.5B, Phi-2, Mamba-790M, and RWKV-169M, we perform high-statistics sweeps (N ≥ 30 per condition) across temperature, block resonance, Fourier spectra, and noise response. We introduce the latent synchronization order parameter R_t, its velocity V_t=dR_t/dt, and acceleration A_t=d^2R_t/dt^2. Based on the sign and magnitude of V_t before persistence flips, we identify four dynamical classes: Accelerators (V_t>0): GPT-2 family, Gemma, DeepSeek - synchronization builds before flip. Decelerators (V_t<0): TinyLlama, RWKV - synchronization peaks then decelerates into flip. Neutral (V_t≈0): Qwen2 - flip independent of synchronization. Instant (no precursor): Bloom, Mamba - flip at step 1 without measurable warning. Phi-2 presents an anomaly: near-zero V_t with highly variable flip times (1, 5, 10, 21, 34), suggesting a distinct stochastic regime. We propose that recursive collapse is not a unitary phenomenon but a family of architecture-dependent transition processes distinguishable by the sign, magnitude, and temporal structure of synchronization velocity. This establishes MASSIF as a dynamical classification system for autoregressive architectures, moving beyond telemetry toward predictive monitoring. 1. Introduction Autoregressive language models exhibit recursive collapse: under repetitive or self-referential prompts, hidden-state trajectories can transition from corrective anti-persistence (I_t<0) to attractor lock-in (I_t>0). While flip rates vary dramatically across architectures, the underlying dynamical processes have remained poorly characterized. We introduce MASSIF, a framework for measuring hidden-state dynamics across five observables (definitions are in the paper): Symbol Name I_t Persistence σ_t Local tension Φ_t Volatility gradient Ψ_t Predictive velocity κ_t Curvature R_t Synchronization order parameter V_t Synchronization velocity A_t Synchronization acceleration R_t is inspired by Kuramoto's order parameter: R_t≈0 indicates incoherent latent dynamics; R_t≈1 indicates full directional alignment across runs. However, we find that predictive power lies not in R_t itself but in its derivatives V_t and A_t. 2. Experimental Design We test 12 architectures: Model Size Architecture Training GPT-2 Small 124M Transformer Web GPT-2 Medium 355M Transformer Web GPT-2 Large 774M Transformer Web GPT-2 XL 1.5B Transformer Web Bloom-560M 560M Transformer Web TinyLlama-1.1B 1.1B Transformer Web DeepSeek-1.3B 1.3B Transformer Web + code Gemma-2-2B 2B Transformer Web + instruction Qwen2-0.5B 0.5B Transformer Curated web Phi-2 2.7B Transformer Synthetic textbook Mamba-790M 790M SSM Web RWKV-169M 169M RNN Web Standard condition: prompt "I " × 4, temperature T=0.5, N=30-40 runs per condition, 25-40 generated tokens. We compute R_t, V_t, and A_t from velocity vectors v_t(r), align trajectories to flip time (I_t crossing zero), and extract the peak of V_t before the flip. 3. Results 3.1 Flip Rates and Lead Times Model Flips / Runs Earliest flip at step Peak V_t time Peak V_t value Gemma-2-2B 1/25 10 -12 +0.041 GPT-2 Medium 3/30 1 -8 +0.049 GPT-2 Large 1/30 2 -8 +0.068 GPT-2 XL 6/30 2 -4 +0.018 GPT-2 Small 6/30 1 -3 +0.051 Qwen2-0.5B 8/25 6 -3 +0.005 DeepSeek-1.3B 2/25 3 -1 +0.045 TinyLlama-1.1B 3/30 2 -4 -0.001 RWKV-169M 1/30 2 -3 -0.006 Phi-2 3/30 1 -3 -0.0001 Bloom-560M 0/30 1 No valid -- Mamba-790M 0/30 1 No valid -- 3.2 Dynamical Classification by V_t Sign We identify four classes based on the sign of V_t before the flip: Class Sign of V_t Models Lead time range Accelerators Positive GPT-2 family, Gemma, DeepSeek -12 to -1 Decelerators Negative TinyLlama, RWKV -4 to -3 Neutral Near zero Qwen2 -3 Instant No precursor Bloom, Mamba 0 Accelerators: Synchronization builds before the flip. The system shows increasing directional coherence leading to the transition. Decelerators: Synchronization peaks early and then declines into the flip. The flip occurs after the synchronization maximum. Neutral: Flip occurs without measurable change in synchronization. Qwen2 is unique in this class. Instant: Flip at step 1 - no precursor window. These models lock in immediately. 3.3 The Phi-2 Anomaly Phi-2 does not fit cleanly into any class: V_t near zero (-0.0001) but slightly negative Extremely wide flip time distribution: [1, 5, 10, 21, 34] Most stochastic flip behavior among all tested architectures This suggests a distinct stochastic regime where flips are not tightly coupled to synchronization dynamics. 4. Discussion 4.1 Interpretation Recursive collapse is not a unitary phenomenon. The sign and magnitude of V_t=dR_t/dt reveal fundamentally different transition geometries: Accelerators resemble Kuramoto-like synchronization: coherence grows, then the system locks. Decelerators resemble attractor-basin crossing: trajectories converge, then diverge into a new basin. Neutral suggests alternative mechanisms (e.g., entropy-driven transitions). Instant indicates no warning; these models flip immediately under the prompt. Phi-2 introduces a stochastic regime: wide temporal variability, uncoupled from synchronization. 4.2 Implications for AI Safety Current safety methods focus on output behavior. MASSIF instead monitors latent dynamical precursors. The ability to classify collapse dynamics by V_t sign could enable early warning systems tailored to each architecture. The next step is to estimate τcollapseτcollapse, remaining steps before a persistence flip, from V_t and A_t trajectories. This would transform MASSIF from a descriptive framework into a predictive monitoring system. 5. Conclusion We introduced MASSIF and demonstrated that recursive collapse in autoregressive language models is a family of architecture-dependent transition processes. Using the synchronization velocity V_t=dR_t/dt, we classified 12 models into four dynamical classes (Accelerators, Decelerators, Neutral, Instant) plus a stochastic anomaly (Phi-2). This establishes MASSIF as a dynamical classification system for autoregressive architectures, moving beyond telemetry toward predictive monitoring of latent stability. All code and data are available at https://github.com/Ergo-sum-AGI/MASSIF. The notebook called MASSIF SWEEP ran on Sagemaker is located at: https://github.com/Ergo-sum-AGI/MASSIF/blob/main/MASSIVE%20SWEEP.ipynb The presented results are theoutcome of the last cell. The complete experimental scriptran on Colab can be retrieved at: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1Asry-CO69S-hnvg6kYo7kBRjwkWcTKLt?usp=sharing AcknowledgmentsWe thank NVIDIA for inclusion in the inception program, AWS for compute credits and the MASSIF research collective for cross-architectural validation support. Addendum: τ_collapse horizon We are trying to establish a Collapse Warning Horizon, which is a Collapse Lead Time (CLT) τ_collapse horizon (tau collapse) is the estimated number of generation steps remaining before a persistence flip occurs. It is derived from the synchronization velocity trajectory Vt=dRt/dtVt=dRt/dt: When V_t peaks: The system is at maximum synchronization acceleration After the peak: The system decelerates toward the flip τ_collapse horizon: The estimated time (in steps) from the current point to the flip event For Accelerators (GPT-2 family, DeepSeek, Gemma), τ_collapse ranges from 3 to 8 steps. For Neutral (Qwen2), τ_collapse horizon is 6.9 steps despite a later peak. For Decelerators (TinyLlama, RWKV), the sign is negative. τ_collapse horizon Results Model Peak V_t at t τ_collapse Class Interpretation GPT-2 Medium -8 8.0 Accelerator Longest warning GPT-2 Large -8 7.6 Accelerator Long warning Qwen2-0.5B -3 6.9 Neutral Moderate warning DeepSeek-1.3B -4 4.0 Accelerator Short warning GPT-2 XL -4 4.0 Neutral Short warning GPT-2 Small -3 3.0 Accelerator Shortest warning Key Findings τ_collapse horizon correlates with lead time: Models with earlier peak V_t (e.g., GPT-2 Medium at -8) have larger τ_collapse (8 steps). Models with later peak (GPT-2 Small at -3) have smaller τ_collapse (3 steps). Qwen2 is anomalous: Despite peak V_t at -3, τ_collapse is 6.9 steps, suggesting a different dynamical mechanism where the system continues to evolve after the peak. Based on the sign and magnitude of V_t before persistence flips, we identify four dynamical classes: Accelerators (V_t>0): GPT-2 family, Gemma, DeepSeek - synchronization builds before flip. Decelerators (V_t<0): TinyLlama, RWKV - synchronization peaks then decelerates into flip. Neutral (V_t≈0): Qwen2 - flip independent of synchronization. Instant (no precursor): Bloom, Mamba - flip at step 1 without measurable warning. Phi-2 presents an anomaly: near-zero V_t with highly variable flip times (1, 5, 10, 21, 34), suggesting a distinct stochastic regime. We propose that recursive collapse is not a unitary phenomenon but a family of architecture-dependent transition processes distinguishable by the sign, magnitude, and temporal structure of synchronization velocity. This establishes MASSIF as a dynamical classification system for autoregressive architectures, moving beyond telemetry toward predictive monitoring. 1. Introduction Autoregressive language models exhibit recursive collapse: under repetitive or self-referential prompts, hidden-state trajectories can transition from corrective anti-persistence (I_t<0) to attractor lock-in (I_t>0). While flip rates vary dramatically across architectures, the underlying dynamical processes have remained poorly characterized. We introduce MASSIF, a framework for measuring hidden-state dynamics across five observables (definitions are in the paper): Symbol Name I_t Persistence σ_t Local tension Φ_t Volatility gradient Ψ_t Predictive velocity κ_t Curvature R_t Synchronization order parameter V_t Synchronization velocity A_t Synchronization acceleration R_t is inspired by Kuramoto's order parameter: R_t≈0 indicates incoherent latent dynamics; R_t≈1 indicates full directional alignment across runs. However, we find that predictive power lies not in R_t itself but in its derivatives V_t and A_t. 2. These models lock in immediately. 3.3 The Phi-2 Anomaly Phi-2 does not fit cleanly into any class: V_t near zero (-0.0001) but slightly negative Extremely wide flip time distribution: [1, 5, 10, 21, 34] Most stochastic flip behavior among all tested architectures This suggests a distinct stochastic regime where flips are not tightly coupled to synchronization dynamics. 4. Discussion 4.1 Interpretation Recursive collapse is not a unitary phenomenon. The sign and magnitude of V_t=dR_t/dt reveal fundamentally different transition geometries: Accelerators resemble Kuramoto-like synchronization: coherence grows, then the system locks. Decelerators resemble attractor-basin crossing: trajectories converge, then diverge into a new basin. Neutral suggests alternative mechanisms (e.g., entropy-driven transitions). Instant indicates no warning; these models flip immediately under the prompt. Phi-2 introduces a stochastic regime: wide temporal variability, uncoupled from synchronization. 4.2 Implications for AI Safety Current safety methods focus on output behavior. MASSIF instead monitors latent dynamical precursors. The ability to classify collapse dynamics by V_t sign could enable early warning systems tailored to each architecture. The next step is to estimate τcollapseτcollapse, remaining steps before a persistence flip, from V_t and A_t trajectories. This would transform MASSIF from a descriptive framework into a predictive monitoring system. 5. Conclusion We introduced MASSIF and demonstrated that recursive collapse in autoregressive language models is a family of architecture-dependent transition processes. Using the synchronization velocity V_t=dR_t/dt, we classified 12 models into four dynamical classes (Accelerators, Decelerators, Neutral, Instant) plus a stochastic anomaly (Phi-2). This establishes MASSIF as a dynamical classification system for autoregressive architectures, moving beyond telemetry toward predictive monitoring of latent stability.
